Linear Algebra — 05 · Inner Products, the Spectral Theorem and the SVD

Created2025-09-17|Updated2025-09-17|Mathematics > Linear Algebra
|Post View:

Linear Algebra 02 defined a vector space with only addition and scaling: an abstract vector space has no lengths and no angles until you add them. This post adds them with an inner product — the dot product of Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn is the model — and three big results follow. Orthogonal projection gives the best approximation from a subspace, which is the whole theory of least squares. The spectral theorem says every real symmetric matrix is diagonal in an orthonormal basis — the eigen-story of Linear Algebra 04 with no defective cases and perpendicular eigenvectors. And the singular value decomposition extends that to every matrix, square or not: any linear map is a rotation, a stretch along perpendicular axes, and another rotation. The SVD gives the best low-rank approximation, the pseudoinverse and principal component analysis. This is the last post of the base series; a table at the end lists planned extensions.

Series map: 00 Vectors & Linear Systems → 01 Matrix Algebra, Inverses & LU → 02 Vector Spaces, Basis & Dimension → 03 Linear Maps, Change of Basis & Determinants → 04 Eigenvalues & Diagonalization → 05 Inner Products, Spectral Theorem & SVD (this post).

Learning Outcome

  • State the inner product axioms, and prove the Cauchy–Schwarz and triangle inequalities.
  • Use orthonormal bases: coordinates by inner products, Pythagoras, Parseval.
  • Project onto a subspace, prove the best-approximation property, and run Gram–Schmidt to get A=QRA = QRA=QR.
  • Solve least-squares problems with the normal equations and with QR, and fit a line to data.
  • Recognise orthogonal matrices, state the spectral theorem, and sketch its proof.
  • Test a symmetric matrix for positive definiteness in four equivalent ways, and find the principal axes of a quadratic form.
  • State the SVD, compute it for a 2×22 \times 22×2 example, and read it geometrically as rotate–stretch–rotate.
  • Use the SVD for norms, condition numbers, best low-rank approximation (Eckart–Young), the pseudoinverse and PCA.

Chapter 1 — Inner products and norms

Terminology

  • Inner product on a real vector space VVV — a function ⟨u,v⟩∈R\langle u, v\rangle \in \mathbb{R}⟨u,v⟩∈R that is symmetric, linear in each argument, and positive definite (axioms below).
  • Inner product space — a vector space together with an inner product.
  • Norm ∥v∥=⟨v,v⟩\lVert v\rVert = \sqrt{\langle v, v\rangle}∥v∥=⟨v,v⟩​ — the length of vvv. A unit vector has norm 1.
  • Orthogonal — ⟨u,v⟩=0\langle u, v\rangle = 0⟨u,v⟩=0, written u⊥vu \perp vu⊥v.
  • Orthonormal list — pairwise orthogonal unit vectors.
  • Orthogonal complement W⊥={v:⟨v,w⟩=0 for all w∈W}W^\perp = \{v : \langle v, w\rangle = 0 \text{ for all } w \in W\}W⊥={v:⟨v,w⟩=0 for all w∈W}.
  • Orthogonal matrix — a square real matrix QQQ with QTQ=IQ^TQ = IQTQ=I.

Axioms and examples

An inner product on a real vector space satisfies, for all u,v,wu, v, wu,v,w and scalars ccc:

  1. Symmetry: ⟨u,v⟩=⟨v,u⟩\langle u, v\rangle = \langle v, u\rangle⟨u,v⟩=⟨v,u⟩.
  2. Linearity: ⟨u+cv,w⟩=⟨u,w⟩+c⟨v,w⟩\langle u + cv, w\rangle = \langle u, w\rangle + c\langle v, w\rangle⟨u+cv,w⟩=⟨u,w⟩+c⟨v,w⟩ (and so, by symmetry, linear in the second slot too).
  3. Positive definiteness: ⟨v,v⟩≥0\langle v, v\rangle \ge 0⟨v,v⟩≥0, with equality only for v=0v = 0v=0.

Examples:

  • Dot product on Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn: ⟨x,y⟩=xTy=∑xiyi\langle x, y\rangle = x^Ty = \sum x_i y_i⟨x,y⟩=xTy=∑xi​yi​. This is the default in this post.
  • Weighted dot product: ⟨x,y⟩=∑wixiyi\langle x, y\rangle = \sum w_i x_i y_i⟨x,y⟩=∑wi​xi​yi​ with all wi>0w_i > 0wi​>0. More generally ⟨x,y⟩=xTMy\langle x, y\rangle = x^TMy⟨x,y⟩=xTMy for any symmetric positive definite MMM (Chapter 6).
  • Functions: on C[0,1]C[0,1]C[0,1], ⟨f,g⟩=∫01f(t)g(t) dt\langle f, g\rangle = \int_0^1 f(t)g(t)\,dt⟨f,g⟩=∫01​f(t)g(t)dt. For example ⟨1,t−12⟩=∫01(t−12) dt=0\langle 1, t - \tfrac12\rangle = \int_0^1 (t - \tfrac12)\,dt = 0⟨1,t−21​⟩=∫01​(t−21​)dt=0: the constant 1 and t−12t - \frac12t−21​ are orthogonal, and ∥t−12∥2=112\lVert t - \tfrac12\rVert^2 = \frac{1}{12}∥t−21​∥2=121​.
  • Matrices: ⟨A,B⟩=tr⁡(ATB)=∑i,jaijbij\langle A, B\rangle = \operatorname{tr}(A^TB) = \sum_{i,j} a_{ij}b_{ij}⟨A,B⟩=tr(ATB)=∑i,j​aij​bij​ (the Frobenius inner product).

Over C\mathbb{C}C the symmetry axiom becomes ⟨u,v⟩=⟨v,u⟩‾\langle u, v\rangle = \overline{\langle v, u\rangle}⟨u,v⟩=⟨v,u⟩​ and the standard product is ∑xiyi‾\sum x_i \overline{y_i}∑xi​yi​​; everything below has a complex version with ATA^TAT replaced by the conjugate transpose A∗A^*A∗.

Cauchy–Schwarz and the triangle inequality

Theorem 1 (Cauchy–Schwarz). ∣⟨u,v⟩∣≤∥u∥ ∥v∥\lvert\langle u, v\rangle\rvert \le \lVert u\rVert\,\lVert v\rVert∣⟨u,v⟩∣≤∥u∥∥v∥, with equality if and only if uuu and vvv are linearly dependent.

Proof. If v=0v = 0v=0 both sides are 0. Otherwise, for every real ttt,

0≤∥u−tv∥2=∥u∥2−2t⟨u,v⟩+t2∥v∥2.0 \le \lVert u - tv\rVert^2 = \lVert u\rVert^2 - 2t\langle u, v\rangle + t^2\lVert v\rVert^2. 0≤∥u−tv∥2=∥u∥2−2t⟨u,v⟩+t2∥v∥2.

A quadratic in ttt with positive leading coefficient that is never negative has at most one real root, so its discriminant is ≤0\le 0≤0: 4⟨u,v⟩2−4∥u∥2∥v∥2≤04\langle u, v\rangle^2 - 4\lVert u\rVert^2\lVert v\rVert^2 \le 04⟨u,v⟩2−4∥u∥2∥v∥2≤0. Equality means the discriminant is 0, so for some ttt the quadratic is 0, that is u=tvu = tvu=tv; conversely u=tvu = tvu=tv gives equality directly. ∎

Cauchy–Schwarz makes angles possible: define θ∈[0,π]\theta \in [0, \pi]θ∈[0,π] by cos⁡θ=⟨u,v⟩∥u∥∥v∥\cos\theta = \frac{\langle u, v\rangle}{\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert}cosθ=∥u∥∥v∥⟨u,v⟩​, a number in [−1,1][-1, 1][−1,1]. Example: u=(1,2,2)u = (1, 2, 2)u=(1,2,2), v=(3,0,4)v = (3, 0, 4)v=(3,0,4) have u⋅v=11u \cdot v = 11u⋅v=11, ∥u∥=3\lVert u\rVert = 3∥u∥=3, ∥v∥=5\lVert v\rVert = 5∥v∥=5, so cos⁡θ=11/15\cos\theta = 11/15cosθ=11/15 and θ≈42.8°\theta \approx 42.8°θ≈42.8°.

Theorem 2 (triangle inequality). ∥u+v∥≤∥u∥+∥v∥\lVert u + v\rVert \le \lVert u\rVert + \lVert v\rVert∥u+v∥≤∥u∥+∥v∥.

Proof. ∥u+v∥2=∥u∥2+2⟨u,v⟩+∥v∥2≤∥u∥2+2∥u∥∥v∥+∥v∥2=(∥u∥+∥v∥)2\lVert u + v\rVert^2 = \lVert u\rVert^2 + 2\langle u, v\rangle + \lVert v\rVert^2 \le \lVert u\rVert^2 + 2\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert + \lVert v\rVert^2 = (\lVert u\rVert + \lVert v\rVert)^2∥u+v∥2=∥u∥2+2⟨u,v⟩+∥v∥2≤∥u∥2+2∥u∥∥v∥+∥v∥2=(∥u∥+∥v∥)2, using Cauchy–Schwarz in the middle. Take square roots. ∎

The same expansion gives Pythagoras: if u⊥vu \perp vu⊥v then ∥u+v∥2=∥u∥2+∥v∥2\lVert u + v\rVert^2 = \lVert u\rVert^2 + \lVert v\rVert^2∥u+v∥2=∥u∥2+∥v∥2.

Chapter 2 — Orthogonality and projection

Orthonormal bases

Proposition 3. An orthogonal list of nonzero vectors is linearly independent.

Proof. If ∑civi=0\sum c_i v_i = 0∑ci​vi​=0, take the inner product with vjv_jvj​: every term except cj⟨vj,vj⟩c_j\langle v_j, v_j\ranglecj​⟨vj​,vj​⟩ vanishes, so cj∥vj∥2=0c_j\lVert v_j\rVert^2 = 0cj​∥vj​∥2=0 and cj=0c_j = 0cj​=0. ∎

The same computation shows why orthonormal bases are so convenient. If q1,…,qnq_1, \dots, q_nq1​,…,qn​ is an orthonormal basis, then for every vvv:

v=∑i=1n⟨v,qi⟩ qi,∥v∥2=∑i=1n⟨v,qi⟩2.v = \sum_{i=1}^n \langle v, q_i\rangle\, q_i, \qquad \lVert v\rVert^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n \langle v, q_i\rangle^2. v=i=1∑n​⟨v,qi​⟩qi​,∥v∥2=i=1∑n​⟨v,qi​⟩2.

Coordinates are just inner products — no linear system to solve. The second formula is Parseval's identity.

Orthogonal projection onto a subspace

Let WWW be a subspace with orthonormal basis q1,…,qkq_1, \dots, q_kq1​,…,qk​. The orthogonal projection of vvv onto WWW is

PWv=∑i=1k⟨v,qi⟩ qi.P_W v = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \langle v, q_i\rangle\, q_i. PW​v=i=1∑k​⟨v,qi​⟩qi​.

The residual v−PWvv - P_W vv−PW​v is orthogonal to every qjq_jqj​ (take the inner product and use orthonormality), hence to all of WWW. So every vvv splits uniquely as v=PWv+(v−PWv)v = P_W v + (v - P_W v)v=PW​v+(v−PW​v) with the first part in WWW and the second in W⊥W^\perpW⊥, and dim⁡W+dim⁡W⊥=dim⁡V\dim W + \dim W^\perp = \dim VdimW+dimW⊥=dimV.

Theorem 4 (best approximation). PWvP_W vPW​v is the unique closest point of WWW to vvv: for every w∈Ww \in Ww∈W with w≠PWvw \neq P_W vw=PW​v,

∥v−w∥>∥v−PWv∥.\lVert v - w\rVert > \lVert v - P_W v\rVert. ∥v−w∥>∥v−PW​v∥.

Proof. Write v−w=(v−PWv)+(PWv−w)v - w = (v - P_W v) + (P_W v - w)v−w=(v−PW​v)+(PW​v−w). The first part is in W⊥W^\perpW⊥, the second in WWW, so by Pythagoras ∥v−w∥2=∥v−PWv∥2+∥PWv−w∥2\lVert v - w\rVert^2 = \lVert v - P_W v\rVert^2 + \lVert P_W v - w\rVert^2∥v−w∥2=∥v−PW​v∥2+∥PW​v−w∥2, and the last term is positive when w≠PWvw \neq P_W vw=PW​v. ∎

In matrix form. If QQQ is the n×kn \times kn×k matrix with orthonormal columns qiq_iqi​, then QTQ=IkQ^TQ = I_kQTQ=Ik​ and the projection matrix is P=QQTP = QQ^TP=QQT. If the columns of AAA are any basis of WWW (not orthonormal), then

P=A(ATA)−1AT.P = A(A^TA)^{-1}A^T. P=A(ATA)−1AT.

Every projection matrix satisfies P2=PP^2 = PP2=P and PT=PP^T = PPT=P. Projection onto a single line through aaa is aaTaTa\frac{aa^T}{a^Ta}aTaaaT​; for example the projection of b=(3,0,3)b = (3, 0, 3)b=(3,0,3) onto the line through a=(1,2,2)a = (1, 2, 2)a=(1,2,2) is a⋅ba⋅aa=99a=(1,2,2)\frac{a \cdot b}{a \cdot a}a = \frac{9}{9}a = (1, 2, 2)a⋅aa⋅b​a=99​a=(1,2,2), with residual (2,−2,1)⊥a(2, -2, 1) \perp a(2,−2,1)⊥a.

Common pitfall: ∑⟨v,qi⟩qi\sum \langle v, q_i\rangle q_i∑⟨v,qi​⟩qi​ is the projection only when the qiq_iqi​ are orthonormal. With a non-orthogonal basis, adding up the one-dimensional projections double-counts, and the result is not the closest point. Use A(ATA)−1ATA(A^TA)^{-1}A^TA(ATA)−1AT, or orthonormalise first.

Chapter 3 — Gram–Schmidt and QR

The algorithm

Given independent vectors v1,…,vnv_1, \dots, v_nv1​,…,vn​, Gram–Schmidt produces an orthonormal list q1,…,qnq_1, \dots, q_nq1​,…,qn​ with the same span at every stage: span⁡(q1,…,qj)=span⁡(v1,…,vj)\operatorname{span}(q_1, \dots, q_j) = \operatorname{span}(v_1, \dots, v_j)span(q1​,…,qj​)=span(v1​,…,vj​) for each jjj. At step jjj, subtract from vjv_jvj​ its projection onto the span of the earlier qqq's, then normalise:

wj=vj−∑i<j⟨vj,qi⟩ qi,qj=wj∥wj∥.w_j = v_j - \sum_{i < j} \langle v_j, q_i\rangle\, q_i, \qquad q_j = \frac{w_j}{\lVert w_j\rVert}. wj​=vj​−i<j∑​⟨vj​,qi​⟩qi​,qj​=∥wj​∥wj​​.

wj≠0w_j \neq 0wj​=0 because vjv_jvj​ is not in the span of v1,…,vj−1v_1, \dots, v_{j-1}v1​,…,vj−1​. So every finite-dimensional inner product space has an orthonormal basis.

Worked example. v1=(1,1,0)v_1 = (1, 1, 0)v1​=(1,1,0), v2=(1,0,1)v_2 = (1, 0, 1)v2​=(1,0,1), v3=(0,1,1)v_3 = (0, 1, 1)v3​=(0,1,1).

Then q2=16(1,−1,2)q_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt6}(1, -1, 2)q2​=6​1​(1,−1,2).
  • ⟨v3,q1⟩=12\langle v_3, q_1\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}⟨v3​,q1​⟩=2​1​ and ⟨v3,q2⟩=16\langle v_3, q_2\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt6}⟨v3​,q2​⟩=6​1​, so w3=(0,1,1)−12(1,1,0)−16(1,−1,2)=(−23,23,23)w_3 = (0, 1, 1) - \frac12(1, 1, 0) - \frac16(1, -1, 2) = (-\frac23, \frac23, \frac23)w3​=(0,1,1)−21​(1,1,0)−61​(1,−1,2)=(−32​,32​,32​), and q3=13(−1,1,1)q_3 = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}(-1, 1, 1)q3​=3​1​(−1,1,1).

Check: q1⋅q2=1−1+012=0q_1 \cdot q_2 = \frac{1 - 1 + 0}{\sqrt{12}} = 0q1​⋅q2​=12​1−1+0​=0, q1⋅q3=−1+1+06=0q_1 \cdot q_3 = \frac{-1 + 1 + 0}{\sqrt6} = 0q1​⋅q3​=6​−1+1+0​=0, q2⋅q3=−1−1+218=0q_2 \cdot q_3 = \frac{-1 - 1 + 2}{\sqrt{18}} = 0q2​⋅q3​=18​−1−1+2​=0.

QR factorisation

Gram–Schmidt, written as matrices, is a factorisation. Each vjv_jvj​ is a combination of q1,…,qjq_1, \dots, q_jq1​,…,qj​ only, with coefficients rij=⟨vj,qi⟩r_{ij} = \langle v_j, q_i\ranglerij​=⟨vj​,qi​⟩ (i<ji < ji<j) and rjj=∥wj∥r_{jj} = \lVert w_j\rVertrjj​=∥wj​∥. So

A=QR,A = QR, A=QR,

with QQQ having orthonormal columns and RRR upper triangular with positive diagonal. For the example, R=QTAR = Q^TAR=QTA:

R=(21/21/203/21/6002/3)≈(1.41420.70710.707101.22470.4082001.1547).R = \begin{pmatrix} \sqrt2 & 1/\sqrt2 & 1/\sqrt2 \\ 0 & \sqrt{3/2} & 1/\sqrt6 \\ 0 & 0 & 2/\sqrt3 \end{pmatrix} \approx \begin{pmatrix} 1.4142 & 0.7071 & 0.7071 \\ 0 & 1.2247 & 0.4082 \\ 0 & 0 & 1.1547 \end{pmatrix}. R=​2​00​1/2​3/2​0​1/2​1/6​2/3​​​≈​1.414200​0.70711.22470​0.70710.40821.1547​​.

Watch out: Classical Gram–Schmidt loses orthogonality in floating point when the columns are nearly dependent. Libraries compute QR with Householder reflections (or use modified Gram–Schmidt, which subtracts each projection from the updated vector). The factorisation is the same; the arithmetic is more stable.

Chapter 4 — Least squares

The problem

An overdetermined system Ax=bAx = bAx=b (AAA is m×nm \times nm×n with m>nm > nm>n) usually has no solution: bbb is not in the column space C(A)C(A)C(A). The least-squares solution x^\hat xx^ minimises ∥b−Ax∥\lVert b - Ax\rVert∥b−Ax∥. By Theorem 4, Ax^A\hat xAx^ must be the projection of bbb onto C(A)C(A)C(A), so the residual e=b−Ax^e = b - A\hat xe=b−Ax^ is orthogonal to every column of AAA: ATe=0A^Te = 0ATe=0. That gives the normal equations

ATA x^=ATb.A^TA\,\hat x = A^Tb. ATAx^=ATb.

If the columns of AAA are independent, ATAA^TAATA is invertible (if ATAx=0A^TAx = 0ATAx=0 then xTATAx=∥Ax∥2=0x^TA^TAx = \lVert Ax\rVert^2 = 0xTATAx=∥Ax∥2=0, so Ax=0Ax = 0Ax=0, so x=0x = 0x=0), and x^=(ATA)−1ATb\hat x = (A^TA)^{-1}A^Tbx^=(ATA)−1ATb is unique.

Least squares with QR

If A=QRA = QRA=QR (reduced: QQQ is m×nm \times nm×n), the normal equations RTQTQRx^=RTQTbR^TQ^TQR\hat x = R^TQ^TbRTQTQRx^=RTQTb simplify to

Rx^=QTb,R\hat x = Q^Tb, Rx^=QTb,

solved by back substitution. This is the method used in practice. Forming ATAA^TAATA squares the condition number (Chapter 7), which can destroy half the significant digits; QR avoids it.

Chapter 5 — Orthogonal matrices and the spectral theorem

Orthogonal matrices

A square QQQ with QTQ=IQ^TQ = IQTQ=I has orthonormal columns and Q−1=QTQ^{-1} = Q^TQ−1=QT. It preserves inner products, lengths and angles: (Qx)⋅(Qy)=xTQTQy=x⋅y(Qx)\cdot(Qy) = x^TQ^TQy = x \cdot y(Qx)⋅(Qy)=xTQTQy=x⋅y. Taking determinants, det⁡(Q)2=1\det(Q)^2 = 1det(Q)2=1, so det⁡Q=±1\det Q = \pm 1detQ=±1. In R2\mathbb{R}^2R2 the orthogonal matrices are exactly the rotations (det⁡=1\det = 1det=1) and the reflections (det⁡=−1\det = -1det=−1) of Linear Algebra 03. Products and inverses of orthogonal matrices are orthogonal.

A change of basis to an orthonormal basis uses an orthogonal PPP, so P−1AP=PTAPP^{-1}AP = P^TAPP−1AP=PTAP: no inverse to compute.

The spectral theorem

Theorem 5 (spectral theorem, real symmetric case). If AAA is a real symmetric n×nn \times nn×n matrix (AT=AA^T = AAT=A), then:

  1. all eigenvalues of AAA are real;
  2. eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal;
  3. AAA has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, so A=QΛQTA = Q\Lambda Q^TA=QΛQT with QQQ orthogonal and Λ\LambdaΛ real diagonal.

Conversely, any QΛQTQ\Lambda Q^TQΛQT is symmetric, so a real matrix is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Proof sketch. The key identity is ⟨Ax,y⟩=xTATy=xTAy=⟨x,Ay⟩\langle Ax, y\rangle = x^TA^Ty = x^TAy = \langle x, Ay\rangle⟨Ax,y⟩=xTATy=xTAy=⟨x,Ay⟩.

(1) Let Av=λvAv = \lambda vAv=λv with v∈Cnv \in \mathbb{C}^nv∈Cn nonzero. The number vˉTAv\bar v^TAvvˉTAv equals its own complex conjugate (conjugate it, use that AAA is real, then transpose the 1×11 \times 11×1 result and use AT=AA^T = AAT=A), so it is real. It also equals λ vˉTv=λ∑∣vi∣2\lambda\,\bar v^Tv = \lambda\sum\lvert v_i\rvert^2λvˉTv=λ∑∣vi​∣2, and ∑∣vi∣2>0\sum\lvert v_i\rvert^2 > 0∑∣vi​∣2>0 is real. So λ\lambdaλ is real.

(2) If Av1=λ1v1Av_1 = \lambda_1 v_1Av1​=λ1​v1​ and Av2=λ2v2Av_2 = \lambda_2 v_2Av2​=λ2​v2​, then λ1⟨v1,v2⟩=⟨Av1,v2⟩=⟨v1,Av2⟩=λ2⟨v1,v2⟩\lambda_1\langle v_1, v_2\rangle = \langle Av_1, v_2\rangle = \langle v_1, Av_2\rangle = \lambda_2\langle v_1, v_2\rangleλ1​⟨v1​,v2​⟩=⟨Av1​,v2​⟩=⟨v1​,Av2​⟩=λ2​⟨v1​,v2​⟩, so (λ1−λ2)⟨v1,v2⟩=0(\lambda_1 - \lambda_2)\langle v_1, v_2\rangle = 0(λ1​−λ2​)⟨v1​,v2​⟩=0.

(3) Induction on nnn. By (1) there is a real eigenvalue λ1\lambda_1λ1​ with a unit eigenvector q1q_1q1​. The complement W=q1⊥W = q_1^\perpW=q1⊥​ is mapped into itself: if w⊥q1w \perp q_1w⊥q1​ then ⟨Aw,q1⟩=⟨w,Aq1⟩=λ1⟨w,q1⟩=0\langle Aw, q_1\rangle = \langle w, Aq_1\rangle = \lambda_1\langle w, q_1\rangle = 0⟨Aw,q1​⟩=⟨w,Aq1​⟩=λ1​⟨w,q1​⟩=0. On the (n−1)(n-1)(n−1)-dimensional space WWW, AAA still satisfies ⟨Ax,y⟩=⟨x,Ay⟩\langle Ax, y\rangle = \langle x, Ay\rangle⟨Ax,y⟩=⟨x,Ay⟩, so by induction WWW has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors q2,…,qnq_2, \dots, q_nq2​,…,qn​. Together with q1q_1q1​ this is an orthonormal eigenbasis of Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn. ∎

Worked example. B=(211121112)B = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}B=​211​121​112​​ from Linear Algebra 04 has eigenvalues 4,1,14, 1, 14,1,1. The eigenvector (1,1,1)(1,1,1)(1,1,1) for 4 is automatically orthogonal to the eigenplane x+y+z=0x + y + z = 0x+y+z=0 for 1. Inside that plane, Linear Algebra 04 used (−1,1,0)(-1, 1, 0)(−1,1,0) and (−1,0,1)(-1, 0, 1)(−1,0,1), which are not orthogonal to each other — Gram–Schmidt fixes that. An orthonormal choice is

q1=13(1,1,1),q2=12(1,−1,0),q3=16(1,1,−2),QTBQ=diag⁡(4,1,1).q_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}(1, 1, 1), \quad q_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, -1, 0), \quad q_3 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt6}(1, 1, -2), \qquad Q^TBQ = \operatorname{diag}(4, 1, 1). q1​=3​1​(1,1,1),q2​=2​1​(1,−1,0),q3​=6​1​(1,1,−2),QTBQ=diag(4,1,1).

The spectral decomposition writes AAA as a sum of rank-one projections:

A=λ1q1q1T+λ2q2q2T+⋯+λnqnqnT.A = \lambda_1 q_1q_1^T + \lambda_2 q_2q_2^T + \dots + \lambda_n q_nq_n^T. A=λ1​q1​q1T​+λ2​q2​q2T​+⋯+λn​qn​qnT​.

For BBB: B=4q1q1T+q2q2T+q3q3TB = 4q_1q_1^T + q_2q_2^T + q_3q_3^TB=4q1​q1T​+q2​q2T​+q3​q3T​. Since q2q2T+q3q3T=I−q1q1Tq_2q_2^T + q_3q_3^T = I - q_1q_1^Tq2​q2T​+q3​q3T​=I−q1​q1T​, this is B=I+3q1q1TB = I + 3q_1q_1^TB=I+3q1​q1T​.

Trick: For symmetric matrices, eigenvectors from different eigenvalues are orthogonal for free. You only need Gram–Schmidt inside an eigenspace of dimension 2 or more.

Chapter 6 — Positive definite matrices and quadratic forms

Four equivalent tests

A symmetric matrix AAA is positive definite if xTAx>0x^TAx > 0xTAx>0 for every x≠0x \neq 0x=0, and positive semidefinite if xTAx≥0x^TAx \ge 0xTAx≥0 for every xxx.

Theorem 6. For a real symmetric n×nn \times nn×n matrix AAA, the following are equivalent:

  1. AAA is positive definite;
  2. every eigenvalue of AAA is positive;
  3. every leading principal minor (the determinant of the top-left k×kk \times kk×k block, k=1,…,nk = 1, \dots, nk=1,…,n) is positive (Sylvester's criterion);
  4. elimination without row swaps succeeds with every pivot positive;
  5. A=RTRA = R^TRA=RTR for some invertible RRR — for example the Cholesky factor, upper triangular with positive diagonal.

Proof of 1 ⇔ 2. Write A=QΛQTA = Q\Lambda Q^TA=QΛQT and put y=QTxy = Q^Txy=QTx (a change to the eigenvector basis; y≠0y \neq 0y=0 exactly when x≠0x \neq 0x=0). Then

xTAx=yTΛy=λ1y12+⋯+λnyn2,x^TAx = y^T\Lambda y = \lambda_1 y_1^2 + \dots + \lambda_n y_n^2, xTAx=yTΛy=λ1​y12​+⋯+λn​yn2​,

which is positive for all y≠0y \neq 0y=0 exactly when every λi>0\lambda_i > 0λi​>0. For 5 ⇒ 1: xTRTRx=∥Rx∥2>0x^TR^TRx = \lVert Rx\rVert^2 > 0xTRTRx=∥Rx∥2>0 when x≠0x \neq 0x=0 because RRR is invertible. The links to 3 and 4 go through the LU factorisation of Linear Algebra 01: the kkk-th pivot equals the ratio of the kkk-th and (k−1)(k-1)(k−1)-th leading minors. ∎

Worked example.

K=(2−10−12−10−12).K = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. K=​2−10​−12−1​0−12​​.

  • Leading minors: 222, 4−1=34 - 1 = 34−1=3, det⁡K=4\det K = 4detK=4. All positive.
  • Pivots: 222, 32\frac3223​, 43\frac4334​ — the ratios 21,32,43\frac21, \frac32, \frac4312​,23​,34​ of consecutive minors.
  • Eigenvalues: 2−2≈0.5862 - \sqrt2 \approx 0.5862−2​≈0.586, 222, 2+2≈3.4142 + \sqrt2 \approx 3.4142+2​≈3.414.
  • The quadratic form is a sum of squares: xTKx=2x2−2xy+2y2−2yz+2z2=x2+(x−y)2+(y−z)2+z2x^TKx = 2x^2 - 2xy + 2y^2 - 2yz + 2z^2 = x^2 + (x - y)^2 + (y - z)^2 + z^2xTKx=2x2−2xy+2y2−2yz+2z2=x2+(x−y)2+(y−z)2+z2, which is 000 only when x=y=z=0x = y = z = 0x=y=z=0.

All four tests agree: KKK is positive definite. (This matrix is the second-difference matrix that appears when a differential equation −u′′=f-u'' = f−u′′=f is discretised.)

Common pitfall: Positive entries do not make a matrix positive definite, and negative entries do not prevent it. (1223)\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{pmatrix}(12​23​) has all entries positive but determinant −1-1−1, so its eigenvalues are 2±52 \pm \sqrt52±5​, one of them negative; KKK above has negative entries and is positive definite.

Quadratic forms and principal axes

A quadratic form is q(x)=xTAxq(x) = x^TAxq(x)=xTAx with AAA symmetric (any cross term bxybxybxy is split evenly between the two off-diagonal entries). The spectral theorem rotates the axes so the cross terms disappear.

Worked example. q(x,y)=5x2+4xy+2y2q(x, y) = 5x^2 + 4xy + 2y^2q(x,y)=5x2+4xy+2y2 has A=(5222)A = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}A=(52​22​), with trace 7 and determinant 6, so eigenvalues 666 and 111. Unit eigenvectors: 15(2,1)\frac{1}{\sqrt5}(2, 1)5​1​(2,1) for 6 and 15(−1,2)\frac{1}{\sqrt5}(-1, 2)5​1​(−1,2) for 1. In the rotated coordinates u=2x+y5u = \frac{2x + y}{\sqrt5}u=5​2x+y​, v=−x+2y5v = \frac{-x + 2y}{\sqrt5}v=5​−x+2y​,

q=6u2+v2.q = 6u^2 + v^2. q=6u2+v2.

(Check at (x,y)=(1,0)(x, y) = (1, 0)(x,y)=(1,0): u=2/5u = 2/\sqrt5u=2/5​, v=−1/5v = -1/\sqrt5v=−1/5​, and 6⋅45+15=5=q(1,0)6 \cdot \frac45 + \frac15 = 5 = q(1, 0)6⋅54​+51​=5=q(1,0).) The level curve q=6q = 6q=6 is the ellipse u2+v2/6=1u^2 + v^2/6 = 1u2+v2/6=1: semi-axis 111 along (2,1)(2, 1)(2,1) and 6\sqrt66​ along (−1,2)(-1, 2)(−1,2). The principal axes are the eigenvectors, and the semi-axes are c/λi\sqrt{c/\lambda_i}c/λi​​ for the level q=cq = cq=c. In calculus the same idea classifies critical points: a positive definite Hessian means a local minimum.

Chapter 7 — The singular value decomposition

The theorem

Diagonalization needs a square matrix, and even then it can fail or need complex numbers. The SVD always works.

Theorem 7 (SVD). Every real m×nm \times nm×n matrix AAA of rank rrr can be written as

A=UΣVT,A = U\Sigma V^T, A=UΣVT,

where UUU (m×mm \times mm×m) and VVV (n×nn \times nn×n) are orthogonal and Σ\SigmaΣ is m×nm \times nm×n with diagonal entries σ1≥σ2≥⋯≥σr>0\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_r > 0σ1​≥σ2​≥⋯≥σr​>0 and zeros elsewhere. The σi\sigma_iσi​ are the singular values (uniquely determined by AAA); the columns viv_ivi​ of VVV and uiu_iui​ of UUU are the right and left singular vectors, and Avi=σiuiAv_i = \sigma_i u_iAvi​=σi​ui​.

Proof. ATAA^TAATA is symmetric and positive semidefinite (xTATAx=∥Ax∥2≥0x^TA^TAx = \lVert Ax\rVert^2 \ge 0xTATAx=∥Ax∥2≥0), so by the spectral theorem it has an orthonormal eigenbasis v1,…,vnv_1, \dots, v_nv1​,…,vn​ with eigenvalues λ1≥⋯≥λn≥0\lambda_1 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n \ge 0λ1​≥⋯≥λn​≥0. Exactly rrr of them are positive, because ATAA^TAATA has the same null space as AAA (shown in Chapter 4), hence rank rrr. Put σi=λi\sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i}σi​=λi​​ and, for i≤ri \le ri≤r, ui=Avi/σiu_i = Av_i/\sigma_iui​=Avi​/σi​. These are orthonormal:

ui⋅uj=viTATAvjσiσj=λj vi⋅vjσiσj={1i=j0i≠j.u_i \cdot u_j = \frac{v_i^TA^TAv_j}{\sigma_i\sigma_j} = \frac{\lambda_j\, v_i \cdot v_j}{\sigma_i\sigma_j} = \begin{cases} 1 & i = j \\ 0 & i \neq j. \end{cases} ui​⋅uj​=σi​σj​viT​ATAvj​​=σi​σj​λj​vi​⋅vj​​={10​i=ji=j.​

Extend u1,…,uru_1, \dots, u_ru1​,…,ur​ to an orthonormal basis of Rm\mathbb{R}^mRm. Then Avi=σiuiAv_i = \sigma_i u_iAvi​=σi​ui​ for i≤ri \le ri≤r and Avi=0Av_i = 0Avi​=0 for i>ri > ri>r, which is AV=UΣAV = U\SigmaAV=UΣ, that is A=UΣVTA = U\Sigma V^TA=UΣVT. ∎

Dropping the zero parts gives the compact form A=∑i=1rσiuiviTA = \sum_{i=1}^{r}\sigma_i u_i v_i^TA=∑i=1r​σi​ui​viT​, a sum of rrr rank-one matrices. The SVD also hands you orthonormal bases for all four fundamental subspaces of Linear Algebra 02: v1,…,vrv_1, \dots, v_rv1​,…,vr​ for the row space, vr+1,…,vnv_{r+1}, \dots, v_nvr+1​,…,vn​ for the null space, u1,…,uru_1, \dots, u_ru1​,…,ur​ for the column space, and ur+1,…,umu_{r+1}, \dots, u_mur+1​,…,um​ for the left null space.

Worked example

A=(3045),ATA=(25202025).A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad A^TA = \begin{pmatrix} 25 & 20 \\ 20 & 25 \end{pmatrix}. A=(34​05​),ATA=(2520​2025​).

u1=Av1σ1=(3,9)/235=110(1,3),u2=Av2σ2=(−3,1)/25=110(−3,1),u_1 = \frac{Av_1}{\sigma_1} = \frac{(3, 9)/\sqrt2}{3\sqrt5} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}(1, 3), \qquad u_2 = \frac{Av_2}{\sigma_2} = \frac{(-3, 1)/\sqrt2}{\sqrt5} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}(-3, 1), u1​=σ1​Av1​​=35​(3,9)/2​​=10​1​(1,3),u2​=σ2​Av2​​=5​(−3,1)/2​​=10​1​(−3,1),

A=110(1−331)⏟U(35005)⏟Σ12(11−11)⏟VT.A = \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix}}_{U} \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 3\sqrt5 & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt5 \end{pmatrix}}_{\Sigma} \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}}_{V^T}. A=U10​1​(13​−31​)​​Σ(35​0​05​​)​​VT2​1​(1−1​11​)​​.

Checks: σ1σ2=15=det⁡A\sigma_1\sigma_2 = 15 = \det Aσ1​σ2​=15=detA (here det⁡U=det⁡V=1\det U = \det V = 1detU=detV=1), and σ12+σ22=50=9+0+16+25\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 = 50 = 9 + 0 + 16 + 25σ12​+σ22​=50=9+0+16+25, the sum of the squared entries.

Watch out: The singular values of AAA are not its eigenvalues. This AAA is triangular with eigenvalues 3 and 5, but singular values 6.7086.7086.708 and 2.2362.2362.236. For a symmetric matrix the singular values are the absolute values of the eigenvalues (more generally this holds for normal matrices, those with ATA=AATA^TA = AA^TATA=AAT), and for a positive semidefinite matrix they are exactly the eigenvalues.

Geometry: rotate, stretch, rotate

Read A=UΣVTA = U\Sigma V^TA=UΣVT from right to left as three steps applied to the unit circle:

  1. VTV^TVT is orthogonal: it rotates (or reflects) the plane, carrying v1,v2v_1, v_2v1​,v2​ to e1,e2e_1, e_2e1​,e2​. Here VTV^TVT is rotation by −45°-45°−45°. The circle stays a circle.
  2. Σ\SigmaΣ stretches along the axes by σ1\sigma_1σ1​ and σ2\sigma_2σ2​. The circle becomes an axis-aligned ellipse with semi-axes 6.7086.7086.708 and 2.2362.2362.236.
  3. UUU rotates again, carrying e1,e2e_1, e_2e1​,e2​ to u1,u2u_1, u_2u1​,u2​. Here UUU is rotation by about 71.6°71.6°71.6° (the angle of (1,3)(1, 3)(1,3)).

So every linear map of Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn sends the unit sphere to an ellipsoid (flattened when AAA is singular); the singular values are its semi-axes, the uiu_iui​ their directions, and the viv_ivi​ the unit vectors that land on them. In general UUU and VVV may include a reflection; both can be chosen as rotations exactly when det⁡A≥0\det A \ge 0detA≥0 (for square AAA).

Norms and conditioning

  • Spectral norm: ∥A∥2=max⁡∥x∥=1∥Ax∥=σ1\lVert A\rVert_2 = \max_{\lVert x\rVert = 1}\lVert Ax\rVert = \sigma_1∥A∥2​=max∥x∥=1​∥Ax∥=σ1​ — the longest semi-axis.
  • Frobenius norm: ∥A∥F=∑aij2=σ12+⋯+σr2\lVert A\rVert_F = \sqrt{\sum a_{ij}^2} = \sqrt{\sigma_1^2 + \dots + \sigma_r^2}∥A∥F​=∑aij2​​=σ12​+⋯+σr2​​ (orthogonal matrices do not change it).
  • Condition number of an invertible AAA: κ(A)=σ1/σn\kappa(A) = \sigma_1/\sigma_nκ(A)=σ1​/σn​, the ratio of the longest to the shortest semi-axis. For the example κ=35/5=3\kappa = 3\sqrt5/\sqrt5 = 3κ=35​/5​=3. Solving Ax=bAx = bAx=b can amplify relative errors in bbb by up to κ\kappaκ; since σi(ATA)=σi2\sigma_i(A^TA) = \sigma_i^2σi​(ATA)=σi2​, forming the normal equations squares it. This, and not the size of det⁡A\det AdetA, measures closeness to singularity (Linear Algebra 03, Chapter 7).

Chapter 8 — Using the SVD

Low-rank approximation

Theorem 8 (Eckart–Young, statement). Let A=∑i=1rσiuiviTA = \sum_{i=1}^r \sigma_i u_i v_i^TA=∑i=1r​σi​ui​viT​ and, for k<rk < rk<r, Ak=∑i=1kσiuiviTA_k = \sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i u_i v_i^TAk​=∑i=1k​σi​ui​viT​. Among all matrices BBB of rank at most kkk,

min⁡rank⁡B≤k∥A−B∥2=∥A−Ak∥2=σk+1,min⁡rank⁡B≤k∥A−B∥F=∥A−Ak∥F=σk+12+⋯+σr2.\min_{\operatorname{rank} B \le k}\lVert A - B\rVert_2 = \lVert A - A_k\rVert_2 = \sigma_{k+1}, \qquad \min_{\operatorname{rank} B \le k}\lVert A - B\rVert_F = \lVert A - A_k\rVert_F = \sqrt{\sigma_{k+1}^2 + \dots + \sigma_r^2}. rankB≤kmin​∥A−B∥2​=∥A−Ak​∥2​=σk+1​,rankB≤kmin​∥A−B∥F​=∥A−Ak​∥F​=σk+12​+⋯+σr2​​.

Keep the kkk largest singular triples and drop the rest; nothing of rank kkk does better. For the example,

A1=35 u1v1T=32(1133)=(1.51.54.54.5),A−A1=(1.5−1.5−0.50.5),A_1 = 3\sqrt5\, u_1v_1^T = \frac{3}{2}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1.5 & 1.5 \\ 4.5 & 4.5 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad A - A_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1.5 & -1.5 \\ -0.5 & 0.5 \end{pmatrix}, A1​=35​u1​v1T​=23​(13​13​)=(1.54.5​1.54.5​),A−A1​=(1.5−0.5​−1.50.5​),

and ∥A−A1∥F2=2.25+2.25+0.25+0.25=5=σ22\lVert A - A_1\rVert_F^2 = 2.25 + 2.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 = 5 = \sigma_2^2∥A−A1​∥F2​=2.25+2.25+0.25+0.25=5=σ22​, as the theorem says.

Storage: a rank-kkk approximation of an m×nm \times nm×n matrix needs k(m+n+1)k(m + n + 1)k(m+n+1) numbers instead of mnmnmn. For a 1000×10001000 \times 10001000×1000 greyscale image and k=50k = 50k=50, that is 100 050100\,050100050 numbers instead of 1 000 0001\,000\,0001000000, about 10%. Whether the result looks acceptable depends on how fast the singular values decay.

The pseudoinverse

The Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of A=UΣVTA = U\Sigma V^TA=UΣVT is

A+=VΣ+UT,A^+ = V\Sigma^+U^T, A+=VΣ+UT,

where Σ+\Sigma^+Σ+ is n×mn \times mn×m with 1/σi1/\sigma_i1/σi​ in place of each nonzero σi\sigma_iσi​. It inverts AAA on the row space and sends the left null space to 0. x+=A+bx^+ = A^+bx+=A+b is the least-squares solution of Ax=bAx = bAx=b with the smallest norm — well defined even when AAA is rank-deficient and the normal equations have infinitely many solutions. If AAA has independent columns, A+=(ATA)−1ATA^+ = (A^TA)^{-1}A^TA+=(ATA)−1AT and A+bA^+bA+b is the x^\hat xx^ of Chapter 4; for the line fit, A+b=(−0.5,1.2)A^+b = (-0.5, 1.2)A+b=(−0.5,1.2). If AAA is invertible, A+=A−1A^+ = A^{-1}A+=A−1.

Example. A=(1111)=2 uuTA = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} = 2\,uu^TA=(11​11​)=2uuT with u=12(1,1)u = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 1)u=2​1​(1,1), so A+=12uuT=14(1111)A^+ = \frac12 uu^T = \frac14\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}A+=21​uuT=41​(11​11​). For b=(1,3)b = (1, 3)b=(1,3) (not in the column space), x+=A+b=(1,1)x^+ = A^+b = (1, 1)x+=A+b=(1,1). Every xxx with x1+x2=2x_1 + x_2 = 2x1​+x2​=2 gives the same smallest residual (because Ax=(2,2)Ax = (2, 2)Ax=(2,2), the projection of bbb), and (1,1)(1, 1)(1,1) is the shortest of them.

Principal component analysis

Put NNN data points in Rp\mathbb{R}^pRp as the rows of a matrix and subtract the mean of each column, giving a centred N×pN \times pN×p matrix XXX. The sample covariance matrix is C=1N−1XTXC = \frac{1}{N - 1}X^TXC=N−11​XTX. If X=UΣVTX = U\Sigma V^TX=UΣVT then C=VΣTΣN−1VTC = V\frac{\Sigma^T\Sigma}{N - 1}V^TC=VN−1ΣTΣ​VT, so:

  • the principal directions are the right singular vectors viv_ivi​ (eigenvectors of CCC);
  • the variance along viv_ivi​ is σi2/(N−1)\sigma_i^2/(N - 1)σi2​/(N−1);
  • projecting the data onto v1,…,vkv_1, \dots, v_kv1​,…,vk​ is the best kkk-dimensional summary in the least-squares sense (Eckart–Young applied to XXX).

Worked example. The four points (3,3),(−3,−3),(1,−1),(−1,1)(3, 3), (-3, -3), (1, -1), (-1, 1)(3,3),(−3,−3),(1,−1),(−1,1) already have mean zero. XTX=(20161620)X^TX = \begin{pmatrix} 20 & 16 \\ 16 & 20\end{pmatrix}XTX=(2016​1620​) has eigenvalues 36 and 4 with eigenvectors (1,1)(1, 1)(1,1) and (1,−1)(1, -1)(1,−1), so the singular values of XXX are 6 and 2. The first principal direction is 12(1,1)\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 1)2​1​(1,1) with variance 36/3=1236/3 = 1236/3=12; the second has variance 4/34/34/3. The first component explains 36/(36+4)=90%36/(36 + 4) = 90\%36/(36+4)=90% of the total variance.

Common pitfall: Forgetting to centre the data. Without subtracting the mean, the first "principal component" mostly points at the mean itself. Also scale the columns first when they are in different units, or the largest-unit variable dominates.

4. Is (4223)\begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{pmatrix}(42​23​) positive definite? Use two different tests.

Solution

Leading minors: 4>04 > 04>0 and 12−4=8>012 - 4 = 8 > 012−4=8>0: yes. Eigenvalues: trace 7, determinant 8, so λ=7±49−322=7±172\lambda = \frac{7 \pm \sqrt{49 - 32}}{2} = \frac{7 \pm \sqrt{17}}{2}λ=27±49−32​​=27±17​​, both positive because 17<7\sqrt{17} < 717​<7. Or complete the square: 4x2+4xy+3y2=(2x+y)2+2y24x^2 + 4xy + 3y^2 = (2x + y)^2 + 2y^24x2+4xy+3y2=(2x+y)2+2y2.

5. Find the singular values of E=(221−1)E = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{pmatrix}E=(21​2−1​) and its condition number.

Solution

ETE=(5335)E^TE = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{pmatrix}ETE=(53​35​) has eigenvalues 8 and 2, so σ1=22\sigma_1 = 2\sqrt2σ1​=22​, σ2=2\sigma_2 = \sqrt2σ2​=2​, and κ=2\kappa = 2κ=2. Check: σ1σ2=4=∣det⁡E∣=∣−2−2∣\sigma_1\sigma_2 = 4 = \lvert\det E\rvert = \lvert -2 - 2\rvertσ1​σ2​=4=∣detE∣=∣−2−2∣.

6. Prove that if QQQ is orthogonal then every real eigenvalue of QQQ is ±1\pm1±1, and every singular value of QQQ is 1.

Solution

If Qv=λvQv = \lambda vQv=λv with v≠0v \neq 0v=0, then ∥v∥=∥Qv∥=∣λ∣ ∥v∥\lVert v\rVert = \lVert Qv\rVert = \lvert\lambda\rvert\,\lVert v\rVert∥v∥=∥Qv∥=∣λ∣∥v∥, so ∣λ∣=1\lvert\lambda\rvert = 1∣λ∣=1. Singular values are square roots of the eigenvalues of QTQ=IQ^TQ = IQTQ=I, all equal to 1: an orthogonal map sends the unit sphere to itself.

7. Show that for a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix the SVD and the spectral decomposition coincide, and give a 2×22 \times 22×2 symmetric matrix where they differ.

Solution

If A=QΛQTA = Q\Lambda Q^TA=QΛQT with all λi≥0\lambda_i \ge 0λi​≥0 (sorted in decreasing order), then U=V=QU = V = QU=V=Q and Σ=Λ\Sigma = \LambdaΣ=Λ is a valid SVD. For a symmetric matrix with a negative eigenvalue, such as (1221)\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{pmatrix}(12​21​) (eigenvalues 3,−13, -13,−1), the singular values are 333 and 111: the sign moves into UUU (take u2=−v2u_2 = -v_2u2​=−v2​).

What's next

This completes the base series: from solving Ax=bAx = bAx=b by elimination (post 00) to the SVD, which describes any matrix completely by two orthonormal bases and a list of stretch factors. The table below lists the posts planned to extend the series. The most natural next step is canonical forms — the full proof of the Jordan form stated in Linear Algebra 04 — followed by the numerical side, where the algorithms behind numpy.linalg (LU with pivoting, Householder QR, the QR eigenvalue algorithm, Golub–Kahan SVD) are studied for speed and accuracy.

Planned future extensions

Post Topic What it covers
06 Jordan form and canonical forms generalised eigenvectors, the Jordan form proof, minimal polynomial, rational canonical form, eAte^{At}eAt for defective matrices
07 Numerical linear algebra floating point and conditioning, LU with pivoting, Householder QR, QR eigenvalue algorithm, computing the SVD, iterative solvers (conjugate gradient, GMRES)
08 Linear algebra for machine learning linear regression and ridge regression, PCA in practice, matrix calculus and gradients, low-rank methods, embeddings
09 Tensors and multilinear algebra dual spaces, bilinear forms, tensor products, exterior algebra and the determinant revisited, tensor decompositions
10 Functional analysis preview normed and Hilbert spaces, infinite orthonormal bases and Fourier series, bounded operators, the spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators

References

  • Sheldon Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right, 4th ed., Springer (2024) — Chapter 6 (inner product spaces, Gram–Schmidt, orthogonal projection, least squares) and Chapter 7 (self-adjoint operators, the spectral theorem, positive operators, SVD). Open access at linear.axler.net.
  • Gilbert Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra, 6th ed., Wellesley-Cambridge Press (2023) — orthogonality, projections, least squares, Gram–Schmidt; symmetric and positive definite matrices; the SVD and PCA.
  • Gilbert Strang, Linear Algebra and Learning from Data, Wellesley-Cambridge Press (2019) — the SVD, Eckart–Young, PCA and low-rank approximation from the data-science side.
  • Lloyd N. Trefethen, David Bau III, Numerical Linear Algebra, SIAM (1997) — Lectures 4–5 (SVD), 6–11 (projectors, QR, Gram–Schmidt, Householder, least squares), 12–15 (conditioning and stability).
  • Gene H. Golub, Charles F. Van Loan, Matrix Computations, 4th ed., Johns Hopkins University Press (2013) — the reference for QR, SVD and least-squares algorithms.
  • Roger A. Horn, Charles R. Johnson, Matrix Analysis, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press (2012) — positive definite matrices, the spectral theorem and the SVD with complete proofs.
  • Carl Eckart, Gale Young, "The approximation of one matrix by another of lower rank", Psychometrika 1 (1936), 211–218 — the original low-rank approximation theorem.
  • MIT OpenCourseWare, 18.06 Linear Algebra (Spring 2010), Gilbert Strang — lectures 14–17 (orthogonality, projections, least squares, Gram–Schmidt), 25 and 27 (symmetric and positive definite matrices) and 29 (SVD); and 18.065 Matrix Methods in Data Analysis, Signal Processing, and Machine Learning (Spring 2018).

Note: this post is in progress. Planned additions: complex inner product spaces and unitary matrices, the spectral theorem for normal matrices, a proof of Eckart–Young, a larger PCA example on real data with a scree plot, and a total-least-squares section.
